name: Regulatory Compliance
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: The Law Does Not Care That It Is Decentralized
lesson.summary: Regulators apply existing financial, privacy, and consumer protection law to blockchain systems regardless of their technical design, forcing projects to reconcile pseudonymity and immutability with rules written for centralized, correctable, identity-verified systems.
lesson.body:
A blockchain's technical properties, no central operator, pseudonymous participants, permanently recorded transactions, do not exempt anyone using it from the law. Regulators in most major jurisdictions have made clear that existing legal categories apply: a token that functions like a security is generally regulated as a security, a business that exchanges cryptocurrency for other value is generally regulated as a money services business or a virtual asset service provider, and personal data recorded through blockchain systems is still subject to data protection law such as the EU's GDPR. Decentralization is a technical architecture choice, not a legal exemption.

Two specific compliance regimes come up constantly in this space. Know Your Customer and Anti-Money Laundering rules require financial intermediaries to verify who their customers are and monitor for suspicious transaction patterns, which sits awkwardly against a technology whose addresses, recall Privacy, are pseudonymous by default. In practice the friction gets resolved at the edges: cryptocurrency exchanges, the on-ramps and off-ramps where crypto meets traditional currency, are required to collect identity information from customers, effectively linking a real identity to specific addresses at that boundary, even though the chain itself stays pseudonymous. The Financial Action Task Force's Travel Rule extends this further, requiring virtual asset service providers to share sender and receiver identity information with each other for larger transfers, the same way banks already do for wire transfers.

The other recurring regime is data protection law, most prominently the EU's GDPR, which grants individuals rights over personal data, including the right to have it corrected or erased. This creates a genuine, well documented tension with immutable ledgers: if personal data ends up written directly onto a blockchain, no participant can unilaterally delete it, because doing so would require rewriting history that thousands of independent nodes have already validated and stored. This tension is significant enough that it gets its own dedicated treatment later in this chapter batch, in Right to Be Forgotten.

A concrete example: MiCA, the EU's comprehensive crypto-asset regulatory framework that phased in through 2024 and 2025, requires crypto-asset service providers to be licensed, hold reserves, disclose risks, and meet governance standards, applying banking-style oversight to an industry that was originally pitched as needing none. The lesson for a skeptic is that a system's technical decentralization does not decentralize legal accountability. Someone, a company issuing a token, an exchange, a foundation, is usually still identifiable and reachable enough for regulators to hold responsible, and compliance costs end up reintroducing centralized checkpoints, identity-verified exchanges, licensed custodians, around the edges of otherwise decentralized systems.
